title: Houthis Threaten Jeddah and All Saudi Red Sea Ports as Strikes Escalate
excerpt: The Houthi warning to evacuate Saudi Red Sea ports came hours before the Saudi-led coalition struck Hodeidah, a day after a Houthi drone hit Riyadh's tallest tower and injured at least 11 people.
body:
• Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday that Jeddah and every other Saudi port on the Red Sea coast will be targeted if Saudi Arabia attacks the Yemeni port of Hodeidah.
  • Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree told port workers and nearby residents to evacuate immediately and shipping companies to withdraw their vessels from Saudi Red Sea ports.
  • After the statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it had struck operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed targets in Yemen's Saada and Amran governorates.
  • The exchange follows Tuesday's Houthi drone strike on Riyadh's tallest tower, which injured at least 11 people — the attack our earlier coverage reported, in which two Indians were among the injured.

Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday threatened to strike Jeddah and all of Saudi Arabia's other Red Sea ports if the kingdom carries out its threats against the Yemeni port of Hodeidah, according to Reuters reporting. In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree urged employees, workers and everyone near the Saudi ports to evacuate immediately, and called on shipping companies to withdraw their vessels.

The threat was not left hanging. After Saree's statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it had targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed a number of targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada and Amran, the coalition said in a statement on Wednesday.

Why Hodeidah is the pressure point

Hodeidah, on Yemen's Red Sea coast, is the main port through which food and other essential supplies enter Houthi-controlled northern Yemen — a lifeline for millions in a country heavily dependent on imported food and humanitarian aid. That is what makes the port such a potent bargaining chip: a threat to Saudi Arabia's Red Sea trade answered against the one harbour Yemen's north cannot do without. Saudi Arabia, for its part, has relied heavily on its Red Sea ports, including Jeddah and Yanbu, for key imports and non-oil exports since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in early March, Marine Insight reported.

An escalation ladder, climbed one rung at a time

Wednesday's exchange is the latest step in a confrontation that has been tightening since September. On Tuesday, a Houthi drone struck the tallest tower in Riyadh, injuring at least 11 people according to Saudi authorities; India condemned that attack, and two Indians were among the injured, as our coverage of the Ministry of External Affairs statement reported. The coalition vowed a firm response to the tower strike.

Renewed fighting has intensified since September, when the Houthis advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Since then the Houthis have stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up air strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response. In July, the Houthis had already announced a ban on all shipping to and from Saudi ports, warning that vessels breaking it could be hit with missiles and drones.

What to watch

The immediate question is whether shipping companies act on Saree's evacuation call at Jeddah and the other Saudi Red Sea ports — a withdrawal would squeeze the very import route Saudi Arabia has depended on since March — and whether the coalition's strikes on Hodeidah expand into the sustained operation against the port that the Houthi threat was meant to deter. For the large Indian workforce in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, the direction of travel matters: the conflict's targets have moved in a week from a Riyadh office tower to the kingdom's western ports.
